utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I give an opportunity -- the opportunity to the Simatovic Defence to call its next witness, I'd like to deal with a few procedural matters, and we were informed that the Prosecution wants to raise a procedural matter as well. The first is about scheduling in the week of the 14th of May. Usually we sit on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday, which would mean the 15th, the 16th, and the 17th of May. The session of the 16th is going to be rescheduled to the 14th, which is Monday. And we are preparing for an afternoon session on that Monday, the 14th; then to be followed by 15th, morning session; and the 17th would be an afternoon session most likely. Does this cause any problems as far as the parties are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I -- I mean, I hesitate, because I do have a professional engagement. I'd agreed to speak at a conference organised in Amsterdam, but obviously this takes precedence. But I mention it just in case there's an alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you supposed to speak in the morning or in afternoon, and is it on the Thursday or is it on the Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's on the Monday. May I just check that? I think it was the afternoon, but may I check that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we then -- but again, we have to look at our agendas as well. We might even consider, although I say it with quite a lot of reservation, to sit in the morning, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- again, this obviously takes precedence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, the Chamber would not like to unnecessarily spoil your agenda. Then the next item. I will deliver the reasons for the decision on the urgent Simatovic motion requesting testimony via video-conference link, a decision about the testimony to be given through -- via video-conference link for Witness Opacic, a decision which was delivered on the 6th of March, 2012, with reasons to follow. The decision itself can be found on page 17.981 of the trial transcript. On the 29th of February, 2012, the Simatovic Defence filed an urgent motion requesting that witness Goran Opacic testify via video-conference link. The Defence submitted that the witness was unable to travel to The Hague due to his own disability and the fact that he assisted in the care of his disabled father. On the 1st of March, the Chamber informally instructed the Defence to provide further information regarding the medical condition of the witness and his father. On the 5th of March, the Simatovic Defence provided the requested further information. On the 6th of March, the Prosecution filed a response to the motion, deferring to the discretion of the Chamber. The Stanisic Defence made no submissions in respect of the motion. The Chamber refers to Rule 81 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence which provides that: "At the request of a party or proprio motu, a Judge or a Chamber may order, if consistent with the interests of justice, that proceedings be conducted by way of video-conference link." The Chamber also refers to its previous decisions on testimony via video-conference link. The Tribunal's jurisprudence has identified the following three factors that must be taken into consideration when addressing whether it is in the interest of justice to allow testimony via video-conference link: First, the inability or unwillingness for good reasons of the witness to travel to the Tribunal; secondly, the importance of the expected testimony for the case of the requesting party; and thirdly, the possible prejudice to the right of the accused to confront the witness. With regard to the inability or unwillingness of the witness to travel to the Tribunal, the Chamber considered the information provided by the Simatovic Defence and accepted that Mr. Opacic, having been awarded a hundred per cent disability status and being his disabled father's principal caretaker, was unable or unwilling for good reasons to travel to the Tribunal. As to the testimony's expected importance, the Chamber considered that Mr. Opacic would, inter alia, testify about the Golubic train camp, the Skabrnja operation of November 1991, and the Kula ceremony of 1997, which made his testimony sufficiently important to the case to make it unfair to the Simatovic Defence to proceed without it. Furthermore, the Chamber found that granting the motion would not cause prejudice to the accused Stanisic and his right to confront the witness in cross-examination. In line with the Tribunal's jurisprudence, a video-conference link in effect constitutes an extension of the courtroom to the witness's location and video-conference link testimony should be given the same probative value as testimony presented in the courtroom. And for the foregoing reasons, the Chamber granted the motion as consistent with the interests of justice. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for this decision. I would like to deliver another decision on behalf of the Chamber. I'll deliver the decision on the Stanisic Additional Motion for Admission of Documents into Evidence from the Bar Table. On the 17th of February, 2012, the Stanisic Defence requested admission of three documents from the bar table, in addition to a motion filed on the same date for the admission of 674 documents into evidence. The three documents are 1D1503, 1D4585, and 1D4586. On the 6th of March, 2012, the Chamber granted an extension for the Prosecution's response to the additional motion to the 23rd of March, 2012. On that date, the Prosecution responded to the Stanisic additional motion. The Simatovic Defence did not make any submissions in respect to the additional motion. The three documents have been made available to the Stanisic Defence under Rule 70 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence and are therefore tendered under seal. The documents concern, inter alia, stipulations about the role of the accused Stanisic in the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1993 and 1995. The Stanisic Defence argues that the three documents are highly probative and relevant to its case. It submits that, first, the proffered documents evidence the accused's co-operation with the international community and his contribution to establishment of peace in the region of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and secondly, support the Defence case that the accused Stanisic did not co-operate with the Bosnian Serbs in relation to any alleged criminal purpose. Although it does not accept these conclusions drawn from the documents, the Prosecution does not oppose their admission from the bar table. The Chamber refers to Rule 89(C) of the Tribunal's Rules, which provides that a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. Based on the submissions by the Stanisic Defence, and considering that the Prosecution does not oppose admission, the Chamber finds that the three additional documents are probative and relevant. Moreover, the Stanisic Defence has demonstrated with clarity and specificity where and how each document fits into its case. Therefore, the Chamber grants the motion. The Chamber is also satisfied that the documents were provided under Rule 70 and, therefore, admits the three documents under seal. The Registry is requested to assign exhibit numbers to these documents and inform the Chamber and the parties once it has done so. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I move to the next item. The Chamber would like to inquire whether, as matters stand now, the Prosecution intends to present any rebuttal evidence. If so, the Prosecution should file any request or notification to that effect no later than the 8th of May, 2012. Should the Prosecution decide that it wishes to seek rebuttal evidence for Defence evidence heard or admitted after that day, any such motions should be filed no later than a week after the date of the introduction of such evidence. Any comments on -- any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. None. No comments other than to confirm that we will be seeking to tender some evidence in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. If you would prefer to remain seated when you address the Chamber, you are allowed to do so. Then the next item deals with the re-calling or at least the issue of re-calling Witness Novakovic. In relation to this issue, the Chamber notes that in the Prosecution's motion to re-call Witness Novakovic, which was filed on the 24th of April, 2012, references made to the indications made by the Stanisic Defence that they would not object the re-call of this witness. And I refer in particular to transcript pages 13961, 14024, and 14168 and -169. The Trial Chamber would like to know whether the Stanisic Defence wishes to maintain their preliminary position on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We maintain the position. I think the argument is going to be the parameters. In particular, the Prosecution seek to put to the witness parts of the Mladic diary, and I think we may object to that. I need to look again at the finer detail of the motion, but in short we -- we do not oppose the re-call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any position already by the Stanisic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no objections to the Prosecution request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. So therefore what remains then is the parameters. Mr. Jordash -- well, first of all, I think it's practical for you to know already that there is no opposition. When would we receive further details as to the parameters you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We could send an informal response, I think, by tomorrow or -- sorry, I just forgot whether it's Tuesday today or Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's Tuesday today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Tuesday. By Thursday, if that would help to expedite things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be appreciated. Does the Simatovic Defence wish to make further submissions, although not opposing the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for the details of the Stanisic response. I have no other matters on my list. Ms. Marcus, I was informed that the Office of the Prosecution would like to raise a matter in relation to bar table motions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. On the 10th of April, 2012, the Simatovic Defence filed a notification in which it first informed the Chamber that it would not be calling proposed military expert witness Borojevic and second where it stated "the Defence intends to prepare bar table motion and ask for admission of selection of documents used in Borojevic's report." The Prosecution would like to know when it can expect to receive this bar table motion, bearing in mind that the Borojevic report, as we all well know, had approximately 1600 sources. Even in the Simatovic Defence were to seek to tender only a portion of those, unless the number is very few, the Prosecution will likely need to request more than the two-week response time for such a motion. To the extent any translations are outstanding, of course, this will impact upon the time we need to review and to respond. And finally, Your Honours, a decision on any prospective Simatovic Defence bar table motion, just as with the pending decision on the Stanisic Defence bar table motion, would have an impact on the materials the Prosecution might seek to tender during its rebuttal case. Due to the fact that, by our time estimates, the Defence witnesses may be completed by the third week in May at the latest, the Prosecution wishes to express its concern about timing. I defer to the Chamber, as usual, on matters of scheduling, but I just raise this as a concern. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. It was a question, an expression of concern; the latter is on the record. The first was about when the Prosecution can expect to receive the bar table motion. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have already said that I am very bad at assessing the time that is needed, but after having said we wouldn't use or call expert Borojevic, we started comparing documents that we want to present via bar table motion. We want to see whether they've already been admitted, and we also want to see whether we have translations of these documents. We are doing -- engaged in this procedure, and this also involves other documents we want to present through a bar table motion. We will try and do this as expeditiously as possible, because we are aware of the fact that if we are late, this could be to the detriment of the Defence case. So with your leave, allow me to say that the Defence case is nearing its close. It's in our interest to present this bar table motion as soon as possible, and we will do this as expeditiously as possible, as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, could you give us an indication about whether you are trying to -- whether you are seeking to have all 1600 documents in evidence or 50 or 20 or 500? What's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I think 10 to 20 per cent of those documents, certainly not all of them. Just the most relevant to those parts of our Defence case that we believe they corroborate. It's between 150 and 200 documents. Certainly not all 1600. Just to be clear: I am only talking about the bar table motion regarding Borojevic, that will be one bar table motion; and there will be another one regarding our 65 ter list and those pieces of evidence that have not been admitted yet through witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I would suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That -- I would suggest that as soon as you have made any -- There's apparently a technical problem, because I received the B/C/S translation on channel 4. Therefore I will restart. Mr. Bakrac, I would suggest that as soon as you have identified documents you would like to include in your bar table motion in relation to the Borojevic report, that you immediately inform the Prosecution. That's one. And of course your further bar table motions, you know how to proceed as far as relevance is concerned. You know exactly that it will take some time to both prepare the motion and to present it to the Chamber in the way which we have prescribed. And it will take some time for the Chamber as well. It's -- the Chamber would wish not to be flooded by material on unclear -- on an unclear basis. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I should probably indicate that we intend to file a further bar table motion. In short, we're still trying to get through all the disclosure that's been served over the last -- well, over the course of the trial, in effect, but mainly what's arrived in the last year. I won't burden the Trial Chamber with the amount or the reasons for why it's come at this stage, but there are thousands of documents and we're working our way through them and selecting some which are, in our view, relevant and probative. So we will have them -- we will certainly be filing a motion. We're not sure of the size of it yet. But I thought I'd better alert the Trial Chamber to that. Yes, I think that's all I can say at this moment. Unless, Your Honour, wants further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we would like is to know as soon as possible what the Stanisic Defence intends to do in this respect. And of course volume is one of the issues, and of course good cause for presenting it at this late stage is another matter. I am not going to exhaustively go through all the relevant aspects, but you certainly have alerted the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And so did the Simatovic Defence. And I take it that the Prosecution was alerted as well. I leave it to that at this moment. The only thing we were talking about, you're checking whether translations are available, Mr. Bakrac, in relation to the bar table documents. Where are we as far as the translation of the documents are concerned for the witness who we'll hope to see within a few minutes in this courtroom? There seems to be some disagreement about the availability of underlying documents of the expert report in a language accessible to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have expended quite significant resources and time to try to figure this out, check, and re-check again, and re-check again. At the moment, we're trying to finalise the last verification of the last group of documents that was sent within the past -- between yesterday and today. I believe that there are fewer than ten, and as soon as I have that list, I will share it with the -- with the Simatovic Defence and the Chamber, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I was just -- I was a bit concerned about the divergence between what the Prosecution thought was missing and sometimes, of course, relevant e-mails are sent to Chamber staff. And we are aware of the problem as perceived by the Prosecution, and the Defence notification which was filed on the 10th of April saying that four English translations were pending and that urgent translation of these documents have been requested. But we are all now below ten, although still a small divergence. Let's proceed and see what happens. Any other matter to be raised by the parties after a considerable time of not sitting? If not, is the Simatovic Defence ready to call its next witness, and that is the expert Milan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We are ready to call our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. At the same time, Mr. Petrovic, there is an extensive report of the witness. You nevertheless asked for six hours of examination-in-chief. Would you always be very clear how your questioning relates to the report; that is, what parts of the report are clarified. Because usually if you call an expert witness, if the Prosecution would have accepted the qualifications of the expert and the conclusions, then the report should have spoken for itself. So, therefore, the Chamber wonders what exactly is there to be clarified and what is added to the report. So could you always clearly indicate where we are and avoid repetition with what is found in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will endeavour to do that, and that is how we have conceived our examination, but I want to emphasise that out of this initial estimate of six hours, we will not use all that time. It will certainly be reduced, but I dare not say exactly how much because I don't know how quickly our examination of this witness will proceed, but it will certainly not be the six hours initially announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Petrovic. Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Petrovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic. I would kindly ask you to state your full name for the record, as well as the date and place of your birth.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: My name is Milan Milosevic. I was born on 23rd January, 1958, in Prokuplje. Is this enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. I should like to ask you to look at 2D921.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D921.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, did you create this document, and what exactly is it?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yes. This is my curriculum vitae in which I presented the most important points from my professional career. It's a working biography and personal biography where I included the most important elements of my scientific, of my academic, and professional career.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to tender this CV as a Defence exhibit, and also to look at 2D922.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, the biography, 2D9 -- what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 921, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 921, yes. Receives number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D790, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D790 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what are we looking at now?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: This is my bibliography, that is to say, the list of all the papers, books, articles, and other publications I authored since 1990 to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I also tender the bibliography of Dr. Milan Milosevic as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the bibliography would reserve number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The bibliography with 2D922 will receive number D791, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D791 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, did you, as asked by the Defence team of Mr. Franko Simatovic, make an expert report on the functioning of the system of internal affairs and the security system of the SFRY and the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yes. I provided that expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now display on the screen 2D913.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is this the cover page of the report that you made for the requirements of the Defence of Mr. Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the benefit of Mr. Milosevic, I should kindly like to ask you to provide him with the hard copy so that he can find it easier, if that's acceptable to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I hear of --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- no objections. Therefore, Mr. Milosevic may be provided with a hard copy of his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, in the period between 1983 and 1995, where were you employed, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: In that period I worked at the Republic Secretariat for Internal Affairs of what was then the Socialist Republic of Serbia in the security department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't this found in detail in the paragraph (e) of the witness ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes. That's just my first question, and now I will be asking about things that are not contained in this paper. I just wanted to put this question as an introduction, but of course I agree; what you're saying is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your biography it says that from 1987 to 1992, in addition to working at the MUP of Serbia, you also taught at the higher school of internal affairs. The subject you taught was state security. What were the requirements of a lecturer who wanted to teach this subject?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The statute of the higher school of internal affairs stipulated that a teacher, a lecturer, for that subject had to be a full-time employee in the Ministry of Internal Affairs. So he had to be in active duty in order to teach there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since you were teaching and working in the State Security Service at the same time, tell us when you opted for the academic career and for what reason did you remain in the State Security Service as an employee?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, immediately in 1987 I chose to become a professor. I chose my academic career. But since it was a requirement to become a full-time employee in the State Security Service, I had to remain there until conditions were right for moving somewhere on a permanent basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why this requirement that you be a full-time employee of the service as a prerequisite for teaching this subject?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The thinking was that nobody could be qualified to teach this subject unless they were familiar with it from inside, unless they were working on it in practice. In other words, it was considered that theoretical knowledge was not enough, that practical experience was also needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From 1992 from 1995 [as interpreted] what was the focus of your academic work?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: I was working on my PhD thesis, preparing my doctorate in the area of criminal procedure and criminal law in order to move to the police academy where I also became a full-time employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your biography we see that between 1992 and 1995 your title was independent instructor for the training of personnel in the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia. What were your duties in that particular period?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: This occupation is idiosyncratic because it is administrative work. I was not doing the practical operative work, but administrative work, so my job was to organise professional examinations and certain preparation and education for people who were admitted to work on a trial period, or interns.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did your duties at that time have anything to do with the operative work of the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: I've already said, my job was administrative. It had nothing to do with operative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In that period, did any operative reports or briefs come or pass your desk, or any other papers created within the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: By the very nature of things, it was impossible for any operative reports to reach me in view of the kind of work I was doing. That's simply the way the service was designed. I had no access to anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a collegium, a meeting of the service, at the time or some other large meeting?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: No, I was never at a collegium at that time or any other time. I didn't occupy a very high-ranking position, and I couldn't attend such meetings given my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to a working meeting or some other meeting with Franko Simatovic or Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: No. Given the situation I was in, I couldn't have any professional contact of any kind with them since the duties we had to perform were quite different. There were no common professional interests that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you on friendly terms or did you have another kind of relationship with Stanisic or Simatovic at the time? Before that period or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: No, we weren't friends. We knew each other by sight, so to speak, but we never really socialised, never went out together. We weren't really friends. We did not have close contact with each other. We didn't even meet each other, since we were in various parts of the building. And it wasn't customary for the employees to visit each other on other floors of the building. There had to be other reasons to go there, and there was no professional reason for us to meet up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the professional tasks and duties of Stanisic and Simatovic from 1991 to 1992, given the position that you occupied?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: No. Because of the position I held, I couldn't have known anything about it. And according to the rules of the service, everything that you know is on a need-to-know basis. You only need to have sufficient knowledge to perform your duties. So since the duties I performed were of a different kind, I couldn't have information of the kind you've been referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the administration that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: If you're referring to the 8th Administration, it was Milan Prodanic. He was the chief. It's the personnel administration, of course. The 8th Administration is a personnel administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of terms were you on with Prodanic? Did you attend a meeting with him, did you go to his office?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, we weren't close associates if that's what you have in mind, and naturally we weren't on friendly terms either. He was an officer. When he thought it was necessary, he could call me and assign me a task of some kind. But we didn't co-operate in professional terms, and I didn't have any private contact with him because, well, quite simply, that was the situation. The duties I performed did not require that I had a lot of contact with those who were in charge of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how did this Defence team get in touch with you? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, since I'm a prominent individual, I'm a professor in Serbia, Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm a public figure, in other words, and I've been involved in theoretical research into security and intelligence for a long time, and I therefore assume that the Defence heard about me because I'm a public figure and you can find my name on the internet, et cetera, and that's why they took the decision they took and got in contact with me last spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's now have a look at your expert report. We won't repeat everything that is contained in your report. But on the basis of your report, we'll try and clarify certain matters. We'll refer to your report in order to clarify certain issues. Could we now have a look at paragraph 15 of your report. In paragraph 15 you speak about the Law on the Basic System for State Security. This law was adopted in the SFRY in 1984. Could you tell us what the significance of this law was at the time that the law was adopted? So in 1984.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The law was adopted in 1986, 1986, but it is based on the concept of All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection, and also on the constitution of the SFRY and on the constitutions of the republics and regions. The idea of this -- behind this law was to define the relationship between the federal and republican and regional organs with regard to state security. It didn't go into the details of state security. The law only provided certain general and basic guidelines and norms. Is it necessary for me to go into further detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you the following: In 1984, if I have understood you correctly, this law was the basic law, the fundamental law, on the basis of which the state security system in the SFRY and republics and regions were established. Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we have a look at P2614, article 2, item 3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... document is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the Registrar not to broadcast this document outside the courtroom. We don't have the B/C/S version yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's the second column, the third paragraph. That's the paragraph I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at the bottom of the first page and of the first column, reference is made to certain subjects within the state security system. Given the way these subjects are listed in Article 2, could you tell us in -- within what context are these subjects of importance in order to understand the system of state security established in the SFRY and in the republics and regions?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: I have already said that this law is based on the idea of social self-protection, and this is quite evident in Article 2. Similarly, I'd like to emphasise the fact that the concept of state security concerns to social order established in accordance with the constitution. In Article 2, it says that the security system for the citizens of the SFRY is carried out for all administrative units.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to slow down for the sake of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to speak more slowly so that the interpreters can translate what you are saying. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: This law is a typical example of the idea of social self-protection. It says the protection of the constitutional order is the right and the duty of all of the subjects. This means all the working people and citizens, organisations and working communities, other self-management organisations, and then social and political organisations. This includes political parties at the time. For example, the Communist League, and so on. Then it's also the task of the association of citizens and of social and political communities, which includes the republics and regions and the local self-management system. So they were all subjects concerned with the protection of the social and constitutional order, but the organs of state security were considered to be the professional services concerned with social self-protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the law was established on the following concept: On the concept of communal work. On the basis of the constitution from 1974, on the basis of that concept and on the basis of that law, how were the duties divided when it came to state security? What were the federation's responsibilities, what were the responsibilities of the republics and of the regions? Could you please just answer that, briefly.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, the state security duties were performed in republics and in regions, but at the federal level things had to be harmonised. There was a certain amount of co-ordination and control of the duties performed, of this work that was carried out. And there were also certain duties that were the exclusive responsibility of the federal Ministry of Internal Affairs, the federal SUP, secretariat of the interior, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this law, which is the basic law regulating the sphere of state security, was in force up until when exactly? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It's difficult to say when it ceased to be in force, since when a law is no longer valid -- well, this is not always explicitly stated. It's not necessarily a fact that there's another law that replaces it with other provisions. So perhaps it no longer has any force regardless of fact that there's no new law.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in official terms, how long was this law valid in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly valid right up until the time that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established. So it was in force after 1990, 1991, and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This law, such as it is, was it applicable after the system changed, after a new constitution was adopted after 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, obviously it wasn't applicable in most respects. These subjects, these social subjects, no longer existed, these subjects for social protection. But after 1993 when this law on social self-protection was officially terminated, these subjects of social self-protection were, in fact, no longer relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at the time of the existence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia a law was ever adopted regulating the basics -- or the basic system of state security?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: No, no such law was adopted at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood your testimony correctly, at the time the state security system was based on the provisions of this law. Or, rather, there wasn't really a basic law that would regulate the way in which it functioned, that would regulate its responsibilities and its position in the system of state security.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: There was not a general law that covered this issue, but there were certain other rules and regulations that determined the position, the function, and the organisation of state security in the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have a look at paragraph 16 in your expert report, which deals with the SFRY constitution from April 1991 and it defines the responsibilities of the federation. It also refers to defence and the security of the country. Were laws ever adopted in the SFRY regulating the security system in the country? And as is stated here, it's one of the exclusive responsibilities of the federation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: If you mean protecting the social order when you refer to security, no. No such laws were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's have a look at paragraph 20 in your expert report. In this paragraph it says that the Law on Internal Affairs of the SAP Vojvodina didn't contain a single provision on the responsibilities of the regional secretariat and the republican secretariat for internal affairs. In the context of this law, what were the consequences of the fact that the way in which it was necessary to co-operate with the secretariat, the republican secretariat for internal affairs, was not defined?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, the consequences of that fact were that it was necessary to have an agreement between the federal and republican levels. Between the organs of internal affairs of the republic and of the federation. This was necessary so that they could take certain measures. There was no duty established in law that showed that the region secretariat for internal affairs had to be subordinated, so to speak, to the republican or federal secretariat for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, does this also concern state security duties?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, yes, it does, because at the time the state security system was only regulated and defined by the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 26 of your report, you deal with the Law on Internal Affairs in the Republic of Serbia from the year 1991. And a provision from that law is quoted here, which concerns co-operation with other ministries in the then-SFRY. What is your assessment of this provision on the Law of Internal Affairs in the Republic of Serbia? Is it of an integral or separatist kind in relation to other ministries in other republics and regions of the time?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It's integrational in nature, unifying in nature. It talks about co-operating -- co-operation with other ministries in the federation, and this should be based on the rights and the duties on providing intelligence, on co-operation, and so on and so forth. So I don't see anything that would be a matter of dispute, anything that would reflect separatist tendencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm looking at the time. I don't know whether it's time for a break now. I can see that Mr. Stanisic would also like a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's time for a break. Mr. Petrovic, when following your questions and what I read in the report, then I now and then wondered what I learned in addition to what I read already by listening to the witness. For example, if the text is on the discharge of joint tasks, mutual co-operation, and informing, the idea of separatist tendencies would not, on the basis of this text, even come to my mind. We take a break and we resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue - and apologies, Mr. Milosevic - Mr. Jordash, did I understand well that you are scheduled to lecture at 1.30 on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, moving from morning to afternoon, it doesn't change anything, because either you'll have to leave early and rush to Amsterdam or you'll have to arrive late when we sit in the afternoon. Is there any way that you could, perhaps, move your, if you would -- if you could move in the -- either earlier in the day, or I don't know. I think I've seen a programme of a conference which I couldn't attend because I had to be in court. Therefore, could I -- as matters stand now, our preference to sit in the afternoon is clear. So therefore, if there's any way you could move to another part of the programme, that would be appreciated. Or I don't know whether it's a two-day programme, but whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, it's a one-day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A one-day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a panel, so it's unlikely to move, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- I'll be in touch with them and report back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even if you there would need any support by the Chamber, I may know some of the organisers as well, but, of course, this is not a promise of any -- of any result.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the risk why I, and perhaps you the same, always accept invitations under one general clause, that if attendance here is needed, that I have to be absent. That's ... but, again, we really would like -- we would have liked to assist you. If there's any way out, if we can do anything for you, don't hesitate to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then our apologies, Mr. Milosevic. There was some matters pending from prior to your arrival. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would like to ask you one question which is in a way a follow-up to what we discussed before the break when you told us that in the relevant period from 1991 to 1995 no law was passed governing internal affairs. Do you know if any other law was passed in the same period governing the position and the role of military security services in the SFRY, that is to say, in the Republic of Serbia in 1991/1995?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: I don't think any law was passed in that area in that period, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 28 of your expert report, which says that the security service within the federal secretariat at the time when the FRY was established was organised as ten administrations and two independent departments. Why does it say it was nominally organised?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The State Security Service as part of the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs formally had these organisational units, these administrations and departments; however, at that time the service had by that time significantly broken down. A lot of personnel had left. There were even a lot of cases of people unlawfully taking items away from their work-places. And the service was not simply carrying out the tasks and missions expected of it. There was even insistence on the part of some authorities and chiefs to reduce the service to the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak a little slowly because it is not easy to transcribe or interpret at this rate. I asked why it was nominally organised into two administrations, and the transcript says "nomally" instead of nominally. I hope this is clear now.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: In fact, only one administration operated and that was the VIP security administration, which continued to operate even later out of the former SDB administration. That administration was formed and this administration dealt with VIP security at the state level and the federal level. I'm sorry if I'm speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Paragraph 29, it says on 18 October, 1992, the building of the federal MUP in Kneza Milosa Street was taken over. Was that something done by the MUP of the Republic of Serbia or by the State Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: That's an activity of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. It involved also members of the State Security Service as well as the public security service. The decision was made at the level of the ministry, and it was carried out at the level of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago we were discussing the state of affairs in the federal Ministry of Interior, but bearing in mind your explanation, the one you've just given, could you please tell us why the building of the federal MUP was taken over on 18 October, 1992, in light of what you've just said and also certain other reasons that you may be able to provide?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: In my opinion, the main reason is precisely this: In the territory of Serbia, in the territory of Belgrade, literally across the road from each other there were two buildings of the ministry, and in one of them no work was being done. There were, instead, lots of cases of theft of documents and even valuable paintings, and the chief of the state security also left that service. The then-leadership of Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, was practically financing two administrations, the federal one and the republic one - the federal MUP and the republic MUP; whereas, the federal one was unable to do anything in view of the situation prevailing at the time. On the other hand, there was the problem of available office space. The republic MUP lacked offices and the offices in the other building were going unused, and that's, from what I know, the main reason why this building was taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, being familiar with the structure of both the federal and republic MUP, tell us what was going on with the affiliated services from both the federal and the republic MUP with this take-over?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: They merged and that was a kind of rationalisation. All the staff, all the members of the federal Ministry of the Interior, including the State Security Service, were taken over. They were offered to continue working, and all of them accepted. Out of some organisational unit, some were expanded, some new were created, and a sort of fusion was implemented. These two services became one single new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could this be called a rationalisation drive in the area of internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: In my opinion, absolutely. And it also helped overcome the problem of working on a double track and duplication that had led to a lot of unnecessary costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 30 of your report. It says: After the take-over, the minister of the interior, Zoran Sokolovic, adopted the rules amending the rules of the internal organisation of the state security department in the Ministry of the Interior. Why these new rules were adopted after the take-over to amend the hitherto rules and the internal organisation of the SDB?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: These amendments were made precisely for the reasons I stated in my previous answer. It was necessary to carry out a merger. These new employees, so to speak, had to be assigned to new jobs, and their job specification had to be expanded to enable these people to continue doing the same kind of work in the newly created organisation. If necessary I can explain in more detail. There were, for instance, employees of the car park or the IT section who were taken over from the other building, and they needed to be included in the job specification to enable them to continue to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to take a look at these amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P2369, Article 1, para 1. Pages 2 and 3 in B/C/S and pages 2 and 3 in English. Page 2 in B/C/S, please, and page 2 in English. Page 3 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the previous number of questions to the witness, I'm not sure what the foundation was. We don't -- we don't have it in the report. We don't have a source being cited. Is it based on personal information? I think before we understand this kind of evidence, where it's coming from, it would be good to know what his authority is. What's the foundation for that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all it follows from the legislative consequences of this event. We have described the event, but I'm interested in the legislative consequences, and they are reflected precisely in this document that I want to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a bit of a chicken/egg solution [sic], I'm afraid. Ms. Marcus, first, for my understanding, were you talking about this functioning of the federal SUP, items being taken away, and that, the factual part of it; is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That as well, Your Honour, yes. In addition, that the merger was a kind of rationalisation. In addition to that, the reasons why it was necessary to carry out a merger. All of this demonstrates some kind of knowledge of inside discussions and a background to the legislation, which is not sourced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, your answer says "I'm interested in the legislative consequences." Now, the issue raised by Ms. Marcus is whether these were legislative consequences. And in order to establish that these were consequences, you would need to know what the factual basis is for triggering such legislative changes. To say, "The law has been changed, therefore this must be the reason," is in itself not yet conclusive without further information. And I think that that's mainly what Ms. Marcus is pointing at. I leave it to you whether you want to further explore it or not, but please be aware that without that basis, the Chamber might have more difficulties in adopting any conclusions the expert witness draws. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, a moment ago when we were talking about this process of take-over and the adoption of new rules, could you explain to us what happened with the personnel employed in the federal MUP in terms of their legal status? What was their legal status and what document governed the legal status of those who wanted to continue to work in the republic MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The answer to that question is what I'm looking at. That's the rules amending the rules on the internal organisation of the State Security Service with the Ministry of the Interior, where Article 1 says that: [As read] "The department from that moment on shall also carry out state administration tasks relevant for the protection of the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the prevention of activities aimed at undermining or destroying the constitutionally established order of the FRY on the territory of the republic." That means that they are all included now. They all continued to do their work as before with the provisio that the Republic of Serbia took upon itself the protection of the FRY as well, in terms of those institutions and territories and areas that were within the Republic of Serbia. The Republic of Montenegro did the same on its own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, then, what was the reason why the RDB of the Republic of Serbia began to include protecting federal interests on the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The reason is that the purview of state security was previously exclusively in the -- at the federal level. The problems themselves and the job itself did not disappear, and the Republic State Security Service was the only entity who was able to continue this work. Of course, the State Security Service is only one of the factors, only one of the players, that participated in the protection of the state security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 31 of your report, we read that: [As read] "The organisation of internal affairs on the constitutional basis, as it was then, was never terminated, particularly because member republics were opposed." What is behind this statement? What was the political disagreement that you only briefly touch upon in this paragraph? You only hint at it.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It is well known that the political and state leadership of the Republic of Montenegro did not wish to accept any agreement or any initiative that would lead to any kind of integration, to making anything common within this two-member federation. And that obviously paralyzed the system, because it was still based on consensus decision-making despite the fact that the federation now consisted of only two members, instead of six plus two as it had been until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I seek some clarification, Mr. Petrovic. You asked the witness how the legal status of staff, of personnel, changed. The witness responded by referring to the change in the tasks; that is, that state security would, from that moment on, also deal with federal security matters. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that, then, explains that those who were working for the state security got a broader task. I understood your question to be, but I haven't heard the answer, what happened with the status of those who were working in the federal security before? Were they incorporated in the ranks of state security and were they now working together with the former state security officials in dealing with that broader task? Because we have two groups of personnel: the one is state security, the other one is federal security. You have explained that state security personnel stayed where they were with a broader task, but I have not heard an answer yet on what happened with personnel of the federal security. Were they, again, incorporated in a different organisation? Were they paid by different authority? Did they -- that's unclear what happened with the status of federal security personnel. And I thought that that was, if not your question, at least part of your question. Could you please seek this to be clarified, and perhaps the witness could provide this clarification immediately, having heard my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They all entered the republican SUP. The SUP was expanded and they were included in it. So this is how these changes occurred. I don't know if I have been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this was exactly the missing element in -- for my understanding of the situation. Does that also mean that they were fund by a different budget now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were all financed from the same budget. They were all part of a single organisation, and they were all financed from the budget of the Republic of Serbia. It was, so to speak, a unified, single organisation that they all worked for. It was one state organ. There were no -- there was no longer a dual track system. They no longer had two state organs, only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, I thought that perhaps previously they may have been paid by federal budget and that they now moved into the republican budget, those who moved from the federal state security to the republican state security.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the previous period, from 1974, let's say, onwards, there was the federal secretariat for internal affairs, the federal secretariat for the interior, and it was financed from the federal budget at the time. But during the period that we are talking about, these republics and regions no longer existed, the regions and republics that were formerly part of the federation, and these bodies contributed to the federal budget. So at the time the Republic of Serbia, and to a lesser extent the Republic of Montenegro, could only pay for these services from the federal budget, but I think that things were stream-lined in this matter to avoid this dual-track system, to have less administrative work, and to reduce the expenses incurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: With reference to the question put to you by the Presiding Judge, the rules on the amendment on the rules of organisation, what was the main purpose of these regulations? Why were they adopted within the context of these changes we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, for this very reason, so that these people could somehow be integrated within the system. There were more employees and it was necessary for job specifications to be expanded. There were to be new positions and new staff members for those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So were there new job specifications that meant that there were new positions for people who had been taken over from the federal state security?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After this process of integration had been completed, did a certain part of the federal state security system continue to exist?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: I've already said that under the first administration that was concerned with protection of subjects remained [as interpreted]. It was in existence until about 2001. But it only provided protection for certain individuals at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who financed this administration that remained part of the federal MUP?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It was obviously the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's budget that financed them. The Republic of Serbia and its organs, excise and customs I think were involved, but I'm not really an expert in terms of budgetary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. In paragraph 33 of your expert report, reference is made to the decision of the federal executive council on specifying state security duties discharged by individual federal administration organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 2D989, page 3 in the B/C/S version, and page 2 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in this decision that you have already seen and that is referred to, or, rather, quoted in your report, the duties of the federal secretariat for internal affairs are mentioned. I am interested in the duties described under items 4 and 5 here, and it says that the federal SUP or, rather, the federal state security - and this is on the basis of the decision from 1984 - it collects data and information abroad on activities of foreign intelligence services, and item 5 says it collects intelligence abroad which is of relevance to security and other matters of interest to the SFRY. Mr. Milosevic, this decision is from the year ... Mr. Milosevic, this decision is from the year 1986. The 8th of May, 1986. I want to know whether this decision, item -- under item 4 and 5 on gathering intelligence, I want to know whether this decision can be applied within -- in a context in which the SFRY is disintegrating in 1991 and 1992. So within the context of the breakup of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: I've already answered that question. I said that motivation was very low and the situation, the political situation, was such at the time that the federal service wasn't really capable to act. I don't think they could perform these duties and obtain significant results of any kind, the results that were needed during that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could we please have a foundation for that? Is that based on his own personal experience, is it based on research, is it based on public open sources? What's the foundation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you tell us the basis upon which you made the claim that you just made.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: I made that claim on the basis of my own research. Amongst other things, I published a few articles, a few books in which I dealt with this period. So this claim is the result of my research. It is the result of my understanding of the historical situation, the circumstances under which these events occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. So the federal secretariat -- the federal state security couldn't perform these duties. Does this affect the need for performing these duties in the Republic of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, it's not only that it didn't affect that need. I think the need was even greater for such work. I can provide you with more details, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The duties that are mentioned here under item 4 and item 5, well, item 4 concerns offensive counter-intelligence work. That's what it's called. There was the need for the department to gather intelligence abroad, intelligence on the activities of foreign intelligence services, and their activities had been stepped-up given the breakup of Yugoslavia. They had always performed such duties, but their activities had been stepped up. And then there's gathering intelligence about enemy emigration, that is, co-operating with the internal enemy in trying to topple the state. So new republics - in Croatia, for example - those who emigrated were returning to the countries. Some terrorist, for example, who had been convicted in the Sweden and had been given lengthy sentences for terrorist acts. Under item 5 it says it was necessary to gather abroad intelligence that is relevant to security and other matters of interest to the SFRY. So just prior to the breakup or when the breakup occurred it was naturally necessary to gather as much intelligence as possible on the intentions, reactions, plans of certain foreign countries, above all on neighbouring countries. But also it was necessary to gather intelligence on all other foreign countries. So I think all countries would step up their activities in such a situation. They wouldn't reduce the sort of activities they had to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, since we said that the federal state security could no longer perform those duties, what would the logical solution then be? How could the need to gather this intelligence be satisfied? To gather intelligence that was relevant to the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, intelligence duties and offensive counter-intelligence duties that we have been discussing is intelligence based on certain principles, for example. Based on the principle of professionalism --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but could you just answer my question in terms of the institutions involved. The organ involved in those duties was disbanded, so were those duties to be performed in some other way by some other organ?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, this is what I was going to say. There was a certain principle according to which it was necessary to use the resources available. That's the principle of available resources. Those organs that could perform those duties, that could carry out that task, and this is a task of social importance, well, these organs had to perform those duties. The existing security organs in the territory of Serbia had to take over these duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get back to that later. I'd also like to ask you the following, since we have this up on the screen now. Under item 6, it says: "Collect data and information of relevance ..." So everything that we have said about the tasks under item 4 and 5, is that also applicable to the task we have under item 6?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, we are now going to look at paragraph 35 of your report, that deals with the rules on employment in the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D239.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: These rules were adopted in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see D239.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: These are rules on employment passed in 1990 at the time when the SFRY existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D239. The translation is 1D1276, item 1. Could we see the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll be dealing with these rules later as well. I would just like to ask you: Do these rules apply? What type of rules are they? Are these very specific rules linked to a specific socio-political order, or are they of a general nature? That's the first question. And second: Do they also apply -- did they also apply in the period from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: With the Court's leave, I would like to answer the second question first. The answer is affirmative, of course. Of course they applied. But they applied precisely because they were universal. They were not linked to any specific socio-political order. These rules explained the methodology and the techniques of the work of the State Security Service, and they are more or less the same across the world. They were phrased and formulated in a high-quality manner, and that's why they continued to apply even later. These rules are more or less the same as those governing any other service in the world of this type. To the best of my knowledge, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 of your expert report, where you also deal with these rules, the co-operation between republic and provincial services is mentioned, as well as organising broader investigations and research in order to assess issues of interest to the security of the country. Does this affect what you just said, that these rules are by nature such that, despite these anachronous parts, they were usable and used in 1991 to 1995 as well?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The passages that referred to the techniques of the service, the methods used, nothing could really affect these rules. But they were anachronous and in a way obsolete even at the time when they were adopted. That's indisputable. My opinion is that this part that deals with the techniques of the service was absolutely correct; whereas the other part dealing with relations between provincial and republic services, agreement-reaching, et cetera, that was anachronous even at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll be dealing with paragraph 40 of your expert report. It deals with the services that make up the state security system of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And you mention, in addition to the State Security Service, you mention also the information and documentation service, SID, and the security service in the ministry of foreign affairs, intelligence and security institutions within the Army of Yugoslavia, the intelligence administration, and the security administration. In addition to these services that were part of the state security system of the FRY, were there any other services, or did you list them all?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: I listed all the services that had any tasks related to this area, even if they were defensive functions, such as VIP security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, for the duration of the existence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, were the relations in terms of jurisdiction between these various components of the state security system institutionally solved? Were there any institutional arrangements made for these relations?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Never completely. It was never made quite clear, and if the Court allows, I could explain why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I believe we have the Court's leave for you to explain concisely.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yugoslavia, both the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Federal Yugoslavia before that and even the Kingdom of Yugoslavia before that, had never had any experience with services that did not belong to ministries. There was never a professional -- co-ordinating and controlling professional service, nor was there ever one single professional service that gathered all the information, all the intelligence. There was no national security council or any other such body. Although the legal grounds existed and specific services had specific purviews and jurisdictions clearly defined, there always occurred some intertwining and overlapping complications resulting from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were the consequences of these various overlaps and inconsistencies in the state security system?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: That leads to a certain amount of rivalry and envy and struggle for primacy between various parts of the system. I'm not talking about the Republic of Serbia now, but of the system as a whole. If there is no body that would oversee all that, it's always possible to succumb to some amount of rivalry and fight for leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please begin the question again. It's going very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to take a break, Mr. Petrovic. But you're also invited to restart your question because the interpreters missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the comparative practice in situations where there is more than one service and more than one agency dealing with state security affairs? How do their inter-relationships function in different systems?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: In most countries, they have what I just said we missed. They have a body of political co-ordination and control, where all the intelligence flows in and which somehow unifies the work results of all service, collates this intelligence, and submits it to the political leadership for decision-making. And at the same time, this overseeing body also provides guidelines to services. Sometimes it is an independent body, and sometimes it is a department of a big central service that integrates all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the last sentence in paragraph 40 says: "Inconsistencies in work were particularly manifest between military intelligence and security institutions on the one hand and the state security organs and the member republics on the other hand." Could you clarify which inconsistencies you mean and which consequences you mean?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The result of these inconsistencies is the very fact that there was no body to oversee and regulate all this. There was a rivalry between military security services, especially the military security service, or if you want to call it counter-intelligence service, and the state security services in various republics, especially Montenegro. That rivalry existed all the time and it probably made the results of their work worse than it could have been if there had been unity in the work of all these services, and such unity is provided by the existence of that body that we were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Let's now move to paragraph 52 of your report. It says a new law on the internal affairs of Republic of Serbia was adopted based on the new constitution of Serbia. It was adopted on 17 July, 1991.
