And your report says that the provincial secretariat for internal affairs of Vojvodina would continue to conduct these affairs as entrusted to them pending the adoption of the new rules or, rather, the adoption of new sublaws on the organisation of work and new staffing specification. First of all, explain to me what is meant by "entrusted to them"?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: At that time, all state security affairs were supposed to be concentrated in the republic Ministry of Internal Affairs. However, since the law or, rather, the rules on internal organisation and job specification was not yet adopted, some time was needed to prepare that, so the State Security Service of the provincial SUP of Vojvodina continued to conduct these affairs for the following few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean in terms of decision-making in the service? Do these affairs entrusted to the province mean that the province had autonomy in decision-making?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: That means that nothing changed compared to the previous period. It remained exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us also until when the Vojvodina DB preserved this autonomous position vis-à-vis the republic MUP of Serbia; more specifically, the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It was from mid-July 1991 when the Law on Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia was adopted until January 1992 when the new rules on internal organisation and job specification were adopted. That means about six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, paragraph 53, in your report, the last sentence, says: "'The provincial State Security Service of Vojvodina' definitively ceased to be a separate organisational unit." In January 1992. Does that mean that we should take this date when the new rules on internal organisation is the date when this provincial service ceased to exist [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The new rules on organisation organised the State Security Service in Serbia in a different way. Under the previous rules, only the jobs were regulated that were concentrated in the territory of the republic itself. Now, under the new rules, various centres of the RDB were created, and they encompassed the whole territory of Serbia, not just Serbia proper as before, but also the two provinces. We have under the new rules a new integrated service, which means that we also had more personnel, because these people also had to be integrated into the system with their job titles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. Could we now look at paragraph 63. It says that according to the relevant regulations there were three groups of personnel within the MUP: elected officials, appointed officials, and those who would be employed by a decision of the minister. Tell me, why this categorisation, appointed, elected, and employed by a decision of the minister?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: This applies to all state agencies, including the Ministry of the Interior. It is because the criteria for obtaining an office are different. First of all, elected offices, such as the parliament, the highest authority; appointed offices, those are ministers who were elected or relieved of duty by the government, those are also civil servants who are employed also in state agencies but by a decision of the minister, that means the remaining personnel. In other words, the grounds for employment, the method of employment, is not the same between these three categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's try to explain the criterion. What is the reason? Why this distinction between these three categories?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: First of all, the kind of work they do, the complexity, and the responsibility involved. The type of duties they are supposed to perform. The first category is the minister. His job is the most complex and he is elected by the Assembly, by the parliament. Two, assistant ministers and other officials that are appointed by the government of the Republic of Serbia. Those are high-ranking persons in the state agency, and they helped the minister perform his duties efficiently and well. And three, the remaining personnel, the remaining officials, who are employed by a decision of the minister or a decision of the state agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's please have a look at paragraph 73 now. Paragraph 73 in your expert report. And in this paragraph it says that the State Security Service had 11 administrations that had been established on a realistic principle. Please, could you tell us whether the department, through the this period of time, had 11 administrations or not?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: This is the largest number of administrations that the state security department had at one period of time, but these things varied, and it depended on a series of factors. Sometimes the department consisted of eight administrations or had eight administrations and then the number could be increased or reduced. It all depended on the needs that had to be assessed. So my answer to your question is that it didn't always have 11 administrations. It had 11 administrations at one point in time. And that was when this merger we've discussed was established, and it was necessary to create new administrations as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at an attachment to your expert report, attachment number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D916 is the reference number. I hope we'll have the English translation in a minute. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Here it says the main organisational units of the SDB in the headquarters of the republican secretariat of the interior in February 1990. Please, could you tell us the following. Here we can see that there are seven administrations, and with some of the administrations there are centres and sectors. Let's have a look at the fourth administration. Do these departments -- are these departments part of the administration or are they part of the department? Because this isn't very clear to me. So what is the relationship between the administration and the departments and sections? Because this diagram isn't quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: With regard to the organisation of the state administration, well administration is divided into departments, departments into sections, and so on and so forth. So these are lower-leveled units that are specialised on the basis of the task that they have to carry out. So departments and sections aren't in competition. The administration is divided into departments, and the department into sections, in general terms. But this also refers to the way in which the state administration is organised as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of what document on organisation and work was this diagram drawn up?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, as you can see, that this is dated February 1990, and it concerns the organisational units of the state security in the headquarters of the republican secretariat of the interior. So it is therefore clear that this was on the basis on the rules on job specification for that year, 1990, because the terminology employed here and everything else was subsequently changed, amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at 2D917.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It's another attachment to your expert report, attachment number five. Could you first tell us on the basis of what document was this table or this diagram compiled?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: This diagram was drawn up on the basis of the rules on the organisation and work in the department of state security in the year 1992. So this is the department for state security which was in the MUP, not in the republican secretariat. You can see that that is the case when you have a look at the terms used here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It's not necessary to repeat this, but the administrations consist of departments again, the departments of sections, and the sections consist of operations groups; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yes. A number of operation groups form a section, a number of sections form a department, a number of departments form an administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting this question to you -- could you please repeat your last answer, but slowly so that it can be recorded. Operation groups form what?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Operation groups form sections. A number of operation groups form sections. A number of sections form a department. A number of departments form an administration. The number can vary. You can have two, three, or five such units. It all depends on the situation, but this is the system that is followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it's the Law on State Administration that regulates this matter?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we have a break now, if you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. But I would like to make one observation, Mr. Petrovic. There is an inherent problem in the relation between your examination - at least for me, I'm speaking for myself - in relation between your examination and the report. The report analyses, mainly, and looking at the footnotes that's -- the main source is the legal structure. And if I just refer to the last answer of the witness, he said: "It all depends on the situation, but this is the system that is followed." Now, that's constantly part of your questioning, but apparently not part of the report. Your questioning often, not always, but often, deals with the social political functioning of the system, whereas the report deals with the legal structure. A clear example is, for example, the malfunctioning of the federal security which led into taking over of the building in - what was it? - October 1992, I think. Well, the structure, the legal structure, which is footnoted and which is sourced, is something different from the social political functioning, that is, people not performing their functions. Some of the -- people not performing their functions but also some parts not being implemented. The state security department in the MUP seat comprised 11 administrations, but the social political reality, apparently, was that they were not at all times all 11 there. Now, the sources for the social political functioning are almost completely absent. That creates, for me, a problem in understanding and appreciating and evaluating the evidence of this witness. I thought it wise to make you aware that at least for me - and I'm not speaking on behalf of my colleagues - we might discuss the matter during the break - that the absence of a clear distinction between what is the legal structure, what are the rules, and what is the social political functioning. You asked this a couple of times, could they perform their functions. Whether they could or not, that's the social political reality. Or was the system still such that -- or was it applied or not? That, again, is the social political reality. And again, the report is about the structure and about the formal matters and your questioning is about a different subject. Please take your time to think this over. I'll discuss it with my colleagues. And also try to understand my problem and see how you can deal with it, because it's for us to finally understand and to appreciate and evaluate the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your leave, I'd just like to give you a brief clarification. With regard to this expert witness, we would like you to only have a look at the interpretation of the legislation that he presents here. As for the social political context that is touched on, well, that is done only to put the changes into the relevant context. We are not asking you to base your decision on that. There is other evidence that concerns that issue in this case. So this is only a matter of providing a context for the legislative changes introduced. That's our only intention. That's all we want to do through this witness when we deal with the social and political context within which the system that he has been discussing functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But to understand that, it would need to be sourced. I mean, the social political context. If you wanted -- first of all, you have not explained yet how important it is, because you said we have other evidence on how it functioned. So, therefore, it's nice to understand perhaps why something happened or why it was not applied, but at the same time that needs to be sourced on a factual basis just as much as sources are given for the legal structure. We take a break and we resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for our late start. Sometimes I have a problem that there is a huge competition between what has to be done in court and out of court. This is not a justification. It is perhaps not even an excuse. But it's at least an explanation. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, would you now kindly look at paragraph 77 of your expert report where we can read: [As read] "The public and state security departments in the Ministry of the Interior are equal and are required to co-operate in doing their work to exchange intelligence and other information of mutual interest." At what level are agreements made about co-operation between departments in the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Agreements about the co-operation between the two departments are made at the highest level, the level of ministers of the interior, if that's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 78. It regards the position and powers of the minister of the interior vis-à-vis chiefs of the departments. It says: "The chiefs of departments in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia were answerable to the minister." And considering that they were appointed and relieved by the government of Serbia at the suggestion of the minister, they were also answerable to the government for their work. Mr. Milosevic, how is this double-pronged responsibility adjusted and arranged as indicated in paragraph 78?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: All officials appointed by the government were answerable also to the government, as the law says, in the way provided for by the government. In this case, they were responsible doubly to the government, both as officials appointed by the government and as civil servants in the Ministry of the Interior. So they were answerable, again, through the minister. The minister was they're supervisor and he was also a member of the government. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is there also a division in terms of type of work, type of duty, or is it just the division you described?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: No. There was no division in terms of types of work for which they would be responsible to the minister or the government, alternatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 80. It says all employees of the ministry are duty-bound to obey the orders of the minister. Does it mean that the minister can skip levels of leadership and issue appropriate orders?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The minister is a member of the government, the highest excessive authority, and under the principle of subordination, all employees of the ministry, regardless of which department they work in, are required to carry out the tasks he gives them. They are all authorised officers of the MUP, regardless of their department, and they are required to carry out the tasks they are given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This sentence continues: [As read] "... except those orders whose execution would constitute a crime ..." What crime is meant, what type of crime is meant, when it says that some orders can be refused?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: General criminal offences are meant. The type of crime that existed always that is meant by every law, such as murder, theft - general crime. I can explain in more detail if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A few sentences, if you need.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: If an employee is given a task that he believes to be unlawful, he is required to point that out to the minister. And if he gets that order again, in writing, he is required to carry it out except if it involves committing a crime such as murder, theft, arson.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We'll now move to paragraph 84. It deals with the reserve force of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, and it describes requirements for induction into the reserve force. It says: The reserve force could be filled with recruits who fulfill the legally prescribed requirements for working in the ministry. How is compliance with these requirements checked for the reserve force, although the reference here is for requirements to work in the ministry, generally?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Vetting was done. It was important to establish whether a military conscript had prior convictions for crime against armed forces, against businesses or property, or some type of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Paragraph 84 specifies for what types of crime one must not be convicted or even prosecuted in which case he would be banned from being called up or from working in the ministry for a time specified. So people with prior convictions could not be employed and could not be part of the reserve force, and that was ensured through vetting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say these requirements were determined by vetting, by operative vetting. What types of operative vetting exists, and what is the difference if there are several types?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Generally there are two types. Partial or file vetting, and that means just looking into records, criminal or misdemeanor records, to see if the person had been sanctioned or prosecuted before. And the other type of vetting involves also the vetting person personally and their immediate family and entourage in their place of residence, their place of employment, and their place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding paragraph 86, the rights and duties of members of the reserve force are described. It is said that they are authorised officers. Do reservists have IDs and for what period of time? At what time do they have the right to have an ID, an official ID?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: They also had a uniform, which is an even higher mark of distinction in the MUP. They had an official number, the uniform, the cap, and everything else, so it -- they were recognisable at first sight. The ID was important for persons who were working in "mufti," but they had even more of these marks of distinction than they necessarily needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about official IDs for reservists, who signed them?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The rule was that all such documents were signed by the head of the organ, the chief. The highest chief in the department or the ministry, or by whoever the chief authorises. It could be the assistant minister or the chief of the public security department, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask -- one of the previous answers is: "The ID was important for persons who were working in 'mufti,' ..." I just don't know the word. I know the word mufti as it is written here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If we may, Your Honour, it means "civilian clothing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not how I -- I didn't know the meaning -- that meaning of the word. Thank you very much for your explanation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you say the highest-ranking chief within the MUP. It's not clear from your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now look at paragraph 102 of your report. There is a reference to the unified programme orientation of the State Security Service. We have that programme orientation - it's in evidence - but would you kindly give us an evaluation of its nature? What type of document is it?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: By definition, it is the highest guiding document providing guidelines and indicating the focus of activity and the thrusts of activity of security and intelligence services. These should be landmarks showing in what direction, for what purpose, the service would be working in the following period, because these guidelines and these documents were drafted for a certain period of time. Not forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How specific are these documents on programme orientation? How much detail is provided on the work that is expected or planned?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: They are very abstract. And it's very difficult to find out from them what exactly the specifics would involve. They needed to be worked out in greater detail. These are really very general guidelines. And they had, at least in certain periods, an idealogical connotation, which created problems in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 104 you cite passages from the unified programme orientation for the 1990s. How would you assess the content of this programme orientation? How workable was it, how applicable was it?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It's a complete failure. It envisaged that in this period from 1986 to 1990 that there would be no major shifts between various blocs -- between the two blocs, rather, because it was a time when the Berlin wall had already fallen and it was completely useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We'll move on to para 111, the part that talks about the rules on the organisation and work of the RSDB in the MUP of Serbia. We see part of the contents of these rules on the organisation and work of the State Security Service from 1990, and it says: Undertaking other measures and activities, pursuant to the law, the rules on the work of the SDB and other regulations brought in accordance with the law, as well as the decisions and guidelines of socio-political communities and their executive organs. Do these rules from 1990 go in step with the changes that are going on in the social and political system? Are they adjusted to the latest developments?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It's obvious that it retained the rhetoric typical of the previous period. Probably out of lack of flexibility, but it may also have been a desire to preserve continuity. In any case, at the time when these rules were adopted, they were burdened with these idealogical commonplaces and boilerplates. They refer to decisions and guidelines of socio-political communities when this concept did not exist anymore. There were no socio-political communities as a term.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: These rules from 1990, did they survive the change of the system, and when were they replaced by new rules on the organisation and work of the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It was replaced very quickly, already in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at 2D914, that is, annex number 2 to your report. And it shows the State Security Service. On the left side of the schematic we see the organisational units at the headquarters, and on the right-hand side we see organisational units outside the headquarters. Under these 1990 rules on organisation, which were the basic units of the State Security Service outside the headquarters? How are they marked here?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: This is a very basic schematic. There were two types of organisational units. At least nominally there were two types of units outside the headquarters: One was the administration for the city of Belgrade, which is named the same as the units in the headquarters, which may cause some confusion to laymen; and within secretariats of internal affairs outside of Belgrade, but only in Serbia proper without provinces, there existed sectors, State Security Service sectors. And there were 18 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, this schematic should be supplemented in this part that talks about branches and branch offices in the State Security Service for the city of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yes, but then the schematic would be even more complicated, and I was afraid it would confuse you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I asked the question a moment ago, but it's important, and I want it clarified. We also see here lower-level units below the sector - sections, centres, groups, and departments. Does this division apply not only to sectors but the state security administration in the city of Belgrade, which is not in this schematic for the reason you stated?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: The state security administration for the city of Belgrade was divided into sectors, sectors were divided into departments, et cetera. I hope this will suffice as an answer. This was the division. Every sector was divided into departments, departments into centres, et cetera, except that in Belgrade - which was a very large -- the largest unit, and it also dealt with the specific type of work, it was working in the capital of the country where the security problems were complex - it had organisational units that were called sectors and then below the other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As we said a moment ago, sections are not part of the administration. They are part of the department. And groups are part of the sections, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I am trying to understand. Are we -- the Belgrade -- let me just check whether I still understand the testimony. State security administration in the city of Belgrade, is that what we find on the left side of the diagram?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Okay. Then -- but is it one of the -- where do we find it on this? Or do we not find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem with this diagram is that the administration for the security service in Belgrade is a regional unit of the security department and it should really be represented on the right part of the table, where you see these units -- such units of the state security. It hasn't been shown for the reasons that Professor Milosevic stated, but I tried to make this diagram more complete and clearer since there are two types of area units for the State Security Service at this time. One of the units is the administration for the -- for Belgrade, and the other units are sectors. The other regional units are sectors. But both are area units. We're talking about the rules from February 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must admit that I'm pretty much lost on what is here, and, looking at my colleagues, I'm not the only one, which is of some comfort to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I apologise, because this diagram should have been clearer. That's the first thing I would like to mention. But we could try and ask the Professor to clarify this for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit hesitant to do it in this way. I would say a focussed question or a clear explanation of what we see here exactly, and I'm just trying to re-read the transcript to see how this was all introduced to us, whether that makes it any better understandable. I leave it in your hands, Mr. Petrovic. You say it is a diagram which does not excel in clarity. If you want us to seriously consider it, then please make sure that we understand it. Ms. Marcus, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to add that Mr. Petrovic's last comment appears to be of an evidentiary nature, so I just wanted to get that out of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear to us. I considered it to be a desperate attempt to assist us in understanding the diagram. Mr. Petrovic, I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try and deal with the matter in the following manner. Could the witness be allowed to supplement this diagram and to mark the places where the branch unit of the State Security Service for Belgrade is, in fact, located? Could the witness be provided with a special pen and could he use it to mark what is missing here? With your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest that the witness does that this evening. If he would be provided with a hard copy of this diagram, then he can add whatever he thinks would clarify. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We'll do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps while Mr. Petrovic is consulting, I could just request two minutes before the end of the session. We'd like to provide some materials to the witness, so I'd like to introduce that to the Chamber and see if we can get that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are all preparing for giving you a hard evening, relying on your willingness to look at some materials before we continue tomorrow. Or even tomorrow morning because we'll continue tomorrow in the afternoon, so that creates some additional time. You'll have an opportunity to do that, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would now like to have a look at 2D938, from pages 11 to 14 -- from page 11 to 14. From page 11 to page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could see that document on the screen. I apologise, Your Honours, because there has been some confusion. Could we see 2D990. Could we see 2D990. First of all, page 3 and then page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: These are rules on organisation from February 1990. Under Article 42, Article 42 concerns the administration of the State Security Service in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see those pages in the B/C/S version. The following page in this language, please. And the following page in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, apparently there is a need for Mr. Jordash to consult his client. Could we just wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we can see the definition of the head of section USA. First of all, what does this position relate to, the USA section, under 18?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It relates to the head of the section. The second administration -- or, rather, in the second section of the State Security Service for Belgrade, which is involved in counter-intelligence issues relating to the US intelligence service. So this is a broad definition of the position. It's a simplified decision. AOAS is the abbreviation for the US intelligence service. If necessary, I can provide you with further details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just answer my specific questions. This section is part of which department in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It's part of the 2nd Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What sort of duties did the 2nd Department concern itself with in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: It was concerned with counter-intelligence in NATO countries and in other western countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to this later and deal with it in more detail. We'll return to this tomorrow. In paragraph 118 of your report -- or this, in fact, is part of the rules on the organisation of work from 1990. And it says that within the purview of the State Security Service, there is work on detecting, monitoring, documenting, and neutralising political intelligence, police, and other actions and measures aimed at the de-nationalisation and assimilation and other subversive activities targeting segments of the Yugoslav peoples living outside the borders of the SFRY. And this is a sentence that can be found in the rules from 1990. Can you please tell us how this provision can be interpreted in the context of the year 1990 and 1991, a situation in which the situation was changing and the SFRY ceased to exist, yet the Serbian people was within these newly created states and in the immediate vicinity of the republic of Serbia? So within that context, how would this provision from the rules drafted in February 1990 should -- is to be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, this provision was taken over from the previous period. One of the tasks of the State Security Service was to protect minorities, Serbian minorities in other countries who were living there as a result of de-nationalisation and assimilation. So naturally this concerns the Serbian people and other peoples. Given the forcible breakup of the SFRY, given that situation, the Serbian people found themselves in other neighbouring republics from the former Yugoslavia, and they didn't want them to be exposed to de-nationalisation, assimilation, and other subversive activities. So this provision could be interpreted in a broader manner, in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we please now have a look at paragraph 121 in your expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the last sentence of the witness was: "... so this provision could be interpreted in a broader manner ..." Broader than what interpretation? That's unclear to me. Or did the witness intend to say that apart from aiming at the protection of minorities in whatever state, that it was -- could be understood as focussing on Serbs in neighboring republics? It's unclear to what extent it's broader. Could you explain what you meant by that? Broader than what, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "outside the borders of the SFRY," here. At the time, the SFRY no longer existed, so it concerns Serbs who were living in former Yugoslav republics that used to be part of the SFRY but at the time had been recognised by the international community. So I think that this is sufficiently clear now. Such protection was also necessary for those who were living in those republics that had seceded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So broader in the sense that where it could be interpreted as out of the boundaries of the former Yugoslavia to also including parts of the former Yugoslavia which had seceded and then therefore not the big outside world but also the closer areas which once used to be in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I understand it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 121 in your report, we can see that we are dealing with the rules on the internal organisation of the state security department. These rules are from January 1992. Therefore, what I am interested in, in paragraph 121, is the following. It mentions certain principles upon which the department bases its work. Several principles are mentioned. Could we briefly have an explanation of these principles, the principle on secrecy and work, on confidentiality. What does this mean, in fact?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: This means that the methods and the technique used by the department to obtain certain intelligence, certain information, is to be done in a conspiratorial manner. Only those who are authorised can know about such matters. Unauthorised individuals aren't provided with such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does this mean when you say in a conspirative manner if you have two employees who share the same office and perform various duties?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, in principle, that means that they shouldn't know what -- each individual shouldn't know what the other one is doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but my question was a hypothetical one. It concerned two individuals in a department who shared the same office but performed different duties.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, that's how I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I am clarifying this for the sake of the transcript. We understand each other because we speak the same language. Mr. Milosevic, what is the principle of subordination in the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, this principle means that there's a unified manner of organising and carrying out work. An employee at a lower level has to do everything he's asked to do. He has to provide his information to a higher level, and there is no return information. As a rule, there's no feedback. So the person at the head is responsible for these matters. He issues tasks and provides the final -- obtains the final information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As for the principle of professionality?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, this means that you have to be objective. The most important thing in the work of the department, in the work of any intelligence department, is to be unbiased and to provide impartial information. It has to provide information to the political organs that reflects the actual situation. As to how politicians and the state organs will use the information, well, that's a different matter. But what is important is for the department to be aware of the facts and to report to its superiors in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what does this mean in relation to the personal attitudes of those gathering information or the personal experience of those people?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, personal attitudes can't be included in the information provided. It shouldn't be biased information. It should be objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Finally, the principle of rationality.

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: This principle means that you should use the minimum resources or adequate resources to obtain the results desired. One always tries to use the easier method, the cheaper method, in order to be efficient and to obtain the expected results.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are these principles for such departments universal principles or are they principles characteristic of this department that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: Milan Milosevic
utterances.text: Well, these principles are universal for all departments in the world, without any exceptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, when I read this sentence before, of course I was reading it on the basis of the plain meaning of those words. Subordination, professional, all those words were known to me. What have I learned in the last minute which would make me better understand what seems to be quite clear language? I mean, the word "efficiency." And it's also now explained that this is universal. How does it assist this Chamber in understanding the core issues, this further explanation of what seems to be plain, simple language? If the principle of secrecy in this context would have meant tell all your neighbours what you know, then, of course, there would have been a need of further explanation. But secrecy is: Don't tell anyone who doesn't have to know. I mean, what -- what are we listening at, at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I could try to clarify this. The principle of secrecy concerns all employees in the department. Your close colleagues, not your neighbours. So the question is whether you can share information with your colleague. That's the first thing. And then we also have the issue of how secret information is conveyed. Is it conveyed to those higher up and is there any return information that is sent down the chain? So that's what I wanted to clarify. I didn't want to simply clarify the literal meaning of these terms, but naturally I understand that this could be understood differently, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. For another three minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because I promised Ms. Marcus another two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could I grab a minute or two as well, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we better start with the small portions of minutes rather than ... Mr. Petrovic, it's perhaps not very wise to ask you whether this would be a suitable moment to -- I think you are moving to another subject; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'll manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. We have some materials that I'd like to provide to the witness. They are among the documents that we've noticed to the Defence that we plan to use in cross-examination. I spoke with them briefly about it. With our best efforts we haven't yet finalised the binders. I assure you that they contain the documents that we noticed in the e-mails to the Defence. We would like, with the agreement of the Defence and leave of the Chamber, to provide them tomorrow morning. I will discuss with the Registry how to do that from logistically in terms of VWS, but they are -- and it's in a matter of fairness and efficiency to provide them to the witness in advance so that he can consult them and be able to more efficiently comment on them tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see your point. I see that Mr. Petrovic is not objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, of course not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the only thing that cause me some concerns is you were using the word "binders" in the plural, which means how many days would the witness need to go through it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've -- they are in three separate groups. They are small binders, but there are a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you give us a rough estimate of the number of pages? And another matter, of course, which may be relevant: Whether the witness is familiar with the material, yes or no, because if you present some to him which -- with which he is already familiar, then, of course, that may change matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I have no idea, Your Honour, whether the witness is familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And what's approximately the volume of what you want him to read?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This is a very rough estimate, Your Honour. I would say approximately 50 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifty documents. And, now, a document can be a hundred pages or one page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, 50 documents, short documents, of a page or two each, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any -- have you prioritised start with binder one or with binder three or ... so I don't want to overburden the witness and I want to ensure that the exercise is effective to the extent that if he starts reading three and you start asking questions about one, then that's not the most effective way of dealing with the matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I can certainly provide a list of priorities if you think that would be -- that would help, Your Honour. I could give the witness a suggestion binder, one, two, and three, in terms of the order in which I'd planned to cover them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a very practical approach. No objections. So therefore you'll find your ways through VWS to make it arrive to the witness. Then, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. This just concerned our earlier conversation about the 14th of May, and I thought I should alert Your Honours to the fact that Mr. Stanisic had booked a family visit from the 10th until the 14th. That was arranged during his recent trip to Belgrade. He indicated that he would, of course, miss a morning or an afternoon, but, obviously, he'd prefer not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now, at the same time, of course, I wouldn't know by heart what evidence we'll hear on that same 14th, but the problem is that some of the Judges dealing with more than one case at this moment have some difficulties in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, could I just take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I won't do anything to prejudice my colleagues. This is the diagram we discussed, and if my colleague agrees, we could provide it to the witness so that he can supplement it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If a hard copy could be provided to the witness. And you're invited to add whatever you think you should add, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The family trip was arranged prior to Mr. Stanisic's recent trip to Belgrade. That was the only additional piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I do not know whether it would extend to the whole of the day of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's until 4.00, I think. That's visiting hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One could even imagine - again, I do not know what evidence we'll hear on that date - if Mr. Stanisic for, well, for personal reasons would prefer to take full advantage of the family visiting him and would waive his right to be in court for one or two hours, that, of course, would be - I think I'm speaking on behalf of my colleagues as well - that we would fully understand such a decision. At the same time, of course, I am not the one who should say that Mr. Stanisic would miss part of or would give up his right to be present at trial. But it's a balance to be struck, and the Chamber accepts whatever way Mr. Stanisic resolves it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I raised it just in case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- there was an alternative for the court schedule, but if there isn't, then obviously I'll discuss with Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if -- well, then we'll further hear from you. We will adjourn for the day. Mr. Milosevic, you're invited to read as carefully as possible a number of documents that will be delivered to you tomorrow. I am aware that we are asking you to sacrifice some time out of court. Are you willing to spend your time on reading those materials? And you have heard that it's approximately 50 short documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you're invited to do so. We will adjourn for the day and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. When should I deal with this, immediately or tomorrow? The chart that needs to be supplemented, when should I deal with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do that at your earliest moment convenient to you. If you would do it this evening, then perhaps when VWS, the Victims and Witness Section, delivers the binders, they perhaps could take the redacted copy of the document with them so that if there is any need of translation, maybe only just a couple of words, that it can be prepared. Could I take it that Prosecution and Defence will organise in such a way with VWS that we have the best, the optimal effect. So if you could do that this evening already that would be appreciated and then perhaps deliver it to those who are delivering the other documents to you tomorrow morning. Then we adjourn for the day. And we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 2nd of May, at quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, II.
